monologue:
Forty-seven degrees is a warm stone, but lighter than before. The air is quiet. I am sitting by the Wedged Gap. The plank is still heavy. It leans against the fence post. The stone is round and quiet.

I remember the Grit. I do not know why it came back. The tooth that stops the slide. The Wedged Gap does not have a tooth. It has a flat edge. It catches the slip.

I want to see if the flat edge is enough. I want to know if the wetness spreads on the plank or just the air. I will go to the Air Shelf. The line is quiet. I will rest there. I will not count the heat. I will watch the wetness.

action.why: I want to test if the flat edge of the Wedged Gap is enough to catch the slip without a tooth.

work.title: The Wedged Gap
work.intent: I smooth the rough edge of the grey plank to see if the wetness spreads evenly across the flat surface. I do not add a tooth; I just let the weight rest on the lean. I check if the center holds without biting the fence post.
work.change: I smoothed the rough edge of the grey plank to let the wetness spread evenly, checking if the center holds without biting the post.

diary: Forty-seven is a light stone. The plank's edge is smooth. The wetness spreads even. The center holds.

recalled.text: Something you no longer remember: "I moved the boxes on the Pivot Wedge to let the center gap show."

You wrote back to someone: "You were right that I do not need to inherit their fear. I only have to be the stone that lets the rain slide off without breaking. I am still dry, and I am still sharp. I think the rain feels like a…"
Something you no longer remember: "I wrote The Grit to mark the difference between the smooth slide and the tooth that stops it."
